# Parameters and Design Intent

A parameter is a named number or expression. Parameters turn a model from a
drawing of one object into a family of objects. They are also the best defense
against the "change one dimension and fix twenty sketches" problem.

## What you will learn

- Which dimensions deserve a name.
- How expressions and units work.
- How to build a small standard-stock library.
- How to change a parameter and verify the rebuild.

## Name the numbers that will change

Not every dimension needs a parameter. Parameterize the values that a client,
site, or supplier is likely to change:

- overall height and width;
- post spacing and bay width;
- joist spacing and deck depth;
- wall stud spacing;
- door and window openings;
- material thicknesses;
- clearances and gaps.

Leave one-off details as plain dimensions. A model with two hundred parameters
is as hard to use as one with none.

## A small parameter set for a fence

A useful starting set:

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|-------|---------|
| `post_size` | 90 mm | actual post width and depth |
| `post_height` | 1800 mm | top of post above ground |
| `bay_width` | 2400 mm | post centre to post centre |
| `rail_section_w` | 45 mm | rail thickness |
| `rail_section_h` | 140 mm | rail depth |
| `picket_width` | 140 mm | actual picket width |
| `picket_gap` | 20 mm | gap between pickets |
| `picket_thickness` | 19 mm | actual picket thickness |

Now a 1800 mm fence and a 2100 mm fence are the same model with one value
changed. A 2400 mm bay and a 3000 mm bay are the same model with another.

## Expressions and units

Parameters can be numbers or expressions:

- `bay_width / 2`
- `post_height + 100 mm`
- `picket_width + picket_gap`
- `30 deg`

Keep units explicit when an expression mixes units. A value written as `1800`
inherits the design's display unit; `1800 mm` is unambiguous. Angles are degrees
in expressions even though the kernel stores radians.

::: {.callout-tip}
If an expression refuses to evaluate, simplify it to a single number first.
Then add one operation at a time. Most errors are a unit mismatch or a
reference to a parameter that was renamed.
:::

## Standard stock as a library

You will reuse the same sections across every project. Make a small library of
standard values:

- `stock_2x4_w = 38 mm`, `stock_2x4_h = 89 mm`
- `stock_2x6_w = 38 mm`, `stock_2x6_h = 140 mm`
- `stock_2x8_w = 38 mm`, `stock_2x8_h = 184 mm`
- `stock_4x4 = 89 mm`
- `stock_6x6 = 140 mm`

These names are more meaningful than `d1`, `d2`, `d3`, and they make the model
self-documenting. When a supplier's actual size differs, change the library
value once.

## Design tables for repeated sizes

A design table is a list of parameter sets: one row per variant. Use it when
you need a family of parts rather than a single model:

- fence panels at 1800, 2100, and 2400 mm;
- decks at 3000, 4000, and 5000 mm wide;
- shed walls at 2400 and 3000 mm.

Even a simple table in the chapter is useful:

| Variant | Bay width | Post height | Picket count |
|---------|-----------|-------------|--------------|
| Small | 1800 mm | 1200 mm | 11 |
| Standard | 2400 mm | 1800 mm | 14 |
| Tall | 2400 mm | 2100 mm | 14 |

The counts are examples; recalculate them with the picket/gap formula in
Chapter 11.

## Build along: parameterize the post

1. Open the post from Chapter 1.
2. Add parameters `post_w = 90 mm`, `post_d = 90 mm`, and
   `post_h = 2400 mm`.
3. Replace the sketch dimensions and the extrude distance with those
   parameters.
4. Change `post_h` to 2700 mm and confirm that the post rebuilds.
5. Change it back to 2400 mm.
6. Save as `designs/05-parametric-post.solidcraft`.

## Checks

- Every parameter has a unit or a unitless purpose.
- Changing one parameter does not produce a warning in the timeline.
- The model still has the expected body count.
- The bounding box matches the new values.

## Exercises

1. Add `rail_spacing` and use it to position two rails on a post.
2. Make a fence panel whose picket count is derived from `bay_width`,
   `picket_width`, and `picket_gap`.
3. Build a two-variant design table for a 1800 mm and a 2400 mm panel.
4. Break a parameter on purpose (rename it, or give it the wrong unit) and read
   the error message. Repair it without undoing the whole model.

## Next

Parameters make one part flexible. The next chapter makes many copies of that
part without losing track of which is the source.
